newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Poverty in Yugoslavia rising, reforms essential.
newsitem.headline: Poverty in Yugoslavia rising, reforms essential.

text.p: Yugoslavia's economic situation has pushed one-third of the population down to subsistance level, making radical reforms the only way out of the worsening crisis, analysts said on Tuesday.

"The number of poor has doubled in Yugoslavia since 1990 to some three million, out of which 650,000 are classified as extremely poor," Gordana Matkovic of the Belgrade think-tank Economics Institute said in an interview to Reuters.

"The precondition for cutting poverty over the long term is a rapid development of a modern market economy and resultant improvement of social welfare," said Matkovic, head of the institute's expert team commissioned to prepare the country's Human Development Report for 1997.

The violent break-up of the former Yugoslavia, hyperinflation in 1993 and the war-related 1992-96 U.N. sanctions have cut the GDP per capita at the beginning of this year to $1,600, just over 59 percent of its level in 1989.
Poverty has permeated all social segments but is primarily an urban problem as over 70 percent of the poor live in towns.
"The most affected are the families of industrial workers and miners, and families with children. These groups account for 38 percent of the poor," Matkovic said.
The key factor in the widespread poverty is growing unemployment, which is becoming a long-term problem.
There were some 800,000 officially registered jobless persons in 1996.
"But what is worrying is that some 55 percent of the unemployed have been waiting for a job for more than three years," Matkovic said.
In addition to the registered unemployment, there is also widespread underemployment, which is as high as 770,000 in the economic sector -- almost one-half of its total workforce.
The growth of underemployment is mainly a result of a government ban on laying off workers and closing down enterprises during the sanctions, Matkovic explained.
"Thus the unemployment rate becomes a startling figure, which according to independent estimates ranges from 30 to even close to 50 percent."
But an estimated 600,000 people classified as unemployed or on paid leave are engaged in the grey economy, which in 1996 accounted for more than 40 percent of the GDP.
Some 650,000 refugees and other war-affected persons, who took refuge in Yugoslavia, are in a particularly difficult situation.
"The most vulnerable categories are the 60,000 refugees and war-affected persons living in collective centres."
Another endangered group are the elderly and pensioners.

"Not only because of low and delayed pensions, which in 1996 stood at an average of some $100 per month, but also because of their inability to gain additional income working in grey economy," Matkovic said.
The majority of the elderly depend wholly on the public pension fund, whose financial strength has been sapped by long-term insolvency.
The extremely difficult economic situation in the country, parting with the previous socialist system, call for both economic and social reforms, the report said.

Matkovic said revitalisation of the economy required the country's full return to the world community and foreign financial assistance, but this could not happen while the outer wall of sanctions remained in place.
"But the reforms are a precondition for removing the outer wall (of sanctions). That is a vicious circle."
